issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette: Mr. Thomas, a 77-year-old North American male and retired delivery driver, first presented with symptoms after a traumatic assault several months ago. He was working late one evening, delivering packages in an unfamiliar part of town, when he encountered a group of individuals who attacked him. Mr. Thomas found himself overwhelmed by the sudden violence, unable to defend himself adequately. The assault left him not only physically injured but also deeply shaken mentally. In the weeks following the incident, Mr. Thomas began to experience profound self-doubt and questioned his ability to handle everyday tasks. He had come to believe that he could no longer trust his judgment or act appropriately in dangerous situations. This sense of doubt was compounded by shattered beliefs about the world's safety, leaving him feeling vulnerable and uncertain at every turn. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Mr. Thomas adopted several maladaptive strategies. He found himself eating excessively, often reaching for high-calorie foods that provided temporary relief from his anxiety. Overeating became a means to manage the distress he felt whenever thoughts of the assault surfaced. This behavior was further reinforced by his tendency to keep busy, working tirelessly around the house or taking on additional tasks to distract himself from the trauma. Mr. Thomas's wife noted that he had become increasingly withdrawn and preoccupied with his work, often spending long hours in the garage or completing odd jobs around their home. These behaviors were not just a sign of busyness but also an active attempt to avoid thinking about the assault. He believed that if he thought too much about what happened, he would be unable to handle it. The self-doubt and shattered beliefs continued to influence his behavior. Mr. Thomas had started eating more and more as a way to numb his emotional pain, leading to noticeable weight gain. His preoccupation with keeping busy also extended into his interactions with others. He avoided social gatherings or any situations that might trigger memories of the assault. What frightened him most was the fear of not being able to protect himself again. This constant threat monitoring made it difficult for him to engage in activities he once enjoyed, such as going on walks or attending community events. His wife expressed concern about his increasing isolation and how these behaviors were affecting their relationship. Mr. Thomas finally sought help when his wife insisted that he see a therapist, noting the significant changes in his behavior and mood. He was most afraid of losing control again but hoped that with support, he could regain some sense of normalcy and trust in himself and the world around him. The tightening loop of negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies had become increasingly burdensome, affecting not only his daily life but also his marriage. Through this journey, Mr. Thomas's self-doubt and shattered beliefs continued to reinforce his maladaptive coping mechanisms, making it challenging for him to break the cycle without professional intervention. His current state was one of profound distress, with a deep-seated need for support and understanding as he navigated the aftermath of the assault.
